outputs.L1: In response to the comment by Kenzelmann and Harris, I demonstrate how the continuum theory of spiral multiferroics can be extended to describe general magnetic orders and explain why the microscopic mechanism of magnetically induced ferroelectricity typically renders such extensions unnecessary. This clarifies why a simple model based on a single vector order parameter successfully captures the thermodynamic and magnetoelectric properties of many spiral multiferroics.
outputs.L2: Responding to Kenzelmann and Harris, I explain how continuum models of spiral multiferroics may be extended to encompass arbitrary magnetic ordering. I also show why these extensions are generally unnecessary because of the microscopic origin of magnetically induced ferroelectricity. This accounts for the success of a basic model based on one vector order parameter in capturing both the thermodynamic and magnetoelectric behavior of numerous spiral multiferroics.
outputs.L3: The continuum theory originally developed for spiral multiferroics can, in principle, be generalized to describe a broader range of magnetic ordering patterns. This observation addresses the issues raised in the comment by Kenzelmann and Harris. In most spiral multiferroics, however, such extensions are not required because the microscopic mechanism responsible for magnetically induced ferroelectricity already constrains the relevant coupling between magnetic order and electric polarization. Consequently, a relatively simple phenomenological model based on a single vector order parameter is sufficient in many cases. Despite its simplicity, this model successfully captures both the thermodynamic behavior and the principal magnetoelectric properties of a wide variety of spiral multiferroic materials.
outputs.L4:
A continuum theory of spiral multiferroics can be generalized beyond the usual assumption that the magnetic structure is described by a single complex vector order parameter. General magnetic states may involve several symmetry-related wave vectors, inequivalent magnetic sublattices, higher spatial harmonics, or multiple irreducible magnetic modes. A complete Landau description must therefore introduce the corresponding order parameters and include all symmetry-allowed magnetic, dielectric, and magnetoelectric couplings. Such an extension can describe noncircular spirals, multi-\(q\) structures, commensurate distortions, and other departures from an ideal single-mode helix.

In many materials, however, the microscopic mechanisms responsible for magnetically induced polarization strongly restrict which combinations of these magnetic variables couple to the electric polarization. Mechanisms such as spin-current or inverse Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya coupling make the polarization depend primarily on the vector chirality of neighboring spins, while exchange striction and related effects often involve only a small set of magnetic bilinears. Additional magnetic modes either do not contribute to the uniform polarization, enter only through higher-order corrections, or remain secondary variables whose effects can be absorbed into renormalized phenomenological coefficients. Consequently, the full multi-component continuum theory frequently reduces, for the purposes of thermodynamics and magnetoelectric response, to an effective theory based on one complex vector describing the amplitude, phase, and rotation plane of the spiral.

This reduction explains the broad success of the simple single-vector order-parameter model. Despite the microscopic complexity of real spiral magnets, it captures the principal phase transitions, field-induced reorientation of the spiral plane, dielectric anomalies, and the magnitude and direction of the induced polarization. More elaborate order parameters become essential only when several magnetic modes are independently soft, when distinct sublattices contribute differently to the polarization, or when higher harmonics and multi-\(q\) correlations play an active role. For a wide class of spiral multiferroics, however, microscopic magnetoelectric mechanisms effectively suppress or hide these additional degrees of freedom, leaving the single-vector continuum theory as an accurate and economical description.
outputs.L5: Kenzelmann and Harris approach their work from different perspectives, yet their ideas share a common focus: understanding how people respond to change. This connection creates space for thoughtful discussion, creative solutions, and new ways of seeing familiar challenges. By bringing contrasting experiences together, Kenzelmann and Harris demonstrate how collaboration can turn individual insights into a broader, more meaningful vision.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a response to Kenzelmann and Harris about continuum theories of spiral multiferroics.
counterfactuals.output: We respond to Kenzelmann and Harris’s comments on continuum descriptions of spiral multiferroics. We clarify the symmetry assumptions underlying our free-energy functional and show how the relevant magnetoelectric couplings connect spiral magnetic order to electric polarization. We also distinguish phenomenological symmetry constraints from microscopic mechanisms and address the range of validity of the continuum approximation. These clarifications reconcile the apparent differences between the two approaches while identifying the physical conditions under which their predictions may diverge.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize how the continuum theory of spiral multiferroics can accommodate general magnetic orders and why a single vector order parameter is often sufficient.
counterfactuals.output:
A continuum theory treats the coarse-grained magnetization as a spatially varying vector field, \(\mathbf M(\mathbf r)\), and writes the most general symmetry-allowed Landau–Ginzburg free energy in \(\mathbf M\), its gradients, and the electric polarization \(\mathbf P\). It therefore need not assume a circular, planar, or even single-\(Q\) spiral. Elliptical helices, cycloids, amplitude-modulated states, higher harmonics, and multi-\(Q\) or noncoplanar textures can all be represented through the spatial/Fourier structure of the same field.

For a dominant ordering wavevector,
\[
\mathbf M(\mathbf r)=\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\boldsymbol\psi\,e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}\right],
\]
where the single complex vector \(\boldsymbol\psi=\mathbf a+i\mathbf b\) already contains two real vectors. Their magnitudes and relative orientation specify the spiral plane, ellipticity, phase, and chirality. Thus “one vector order parameter” does not mean one scalar mode or a rigid spin direction; it can encode a very general magnetic order.

Magnetoelectricity then follows from gradient couplings allowed by symmetry, schematically
\[
\mathbf P\cdot\!\left[\mathbf M(\nabla\!\cdot\!\mathbf M)
-(\mathbf M\!\cdot\!\nabla)\mathbf M\right],
\]
or equivalent Lifshitz-invariant forms. Such terms make noncollinear spatial variation induce polarization.

Additional order parameters are needed only when several symmetry-inequivalent magnetic modes—such as independent sublattices, irreducible representations, or unrelated soft wavevectors—must be treated independently. Otherwise, their effects can usually be absorbed into the components and Fourier harmonics of a single coarse-grained vector field.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a brief author reply explaining why microscopic mechanisms of magnetically induced ferroelectricity make modifications to the standard spiral-multiferroic model largely unnecessary.
counterfactuals.output: We thank the reviewer for this comment. Microscopic mechanisms of magnetically induced ferroelectricity—such as the inverse Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (spin-current) interaction and related spin–orbit-driven ligand displacements—lead, after coarse-graining, to the same symmetry-allowed coupling between polarization and spiral magnetic order used in the standard spiral-multiferroic model. Their principal effect is therefore to renormalize effective coupling constants rather than alter the model’s structure. Unless experiments reveal additional symmetry breaking, competing exchange-striction effects, or substantial higher-order contributions, major modifications are neither required nor justified.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In one paragraph, explain the success of a simple single-vector-order-parameter model in describing the thermodynamics and magnetoelectric properties of spiral multiferroics, while addressing Kenzelmann and Harris’s criticism.
counterfactuals.output: A simple model based on a single vector magnetic order parameter succeeds because a spiral is naturally represented by the spatially varying spin vector, while weak anisotropy selects its propagation direction and rotation plane; a symmetry-allowed magnetoelectric coupling of the form \(\mathbf P\!\cdot[\mathbf M(\nabla\!\cdot\!\mathbf M)-(\mathbf M\!\cdot\!\nabla)\mathbf M]\) then yields the observed relation \(\mathbf P\propto \mathbf Q\times\mathbf e\), polarization flops, dielectric anomalies, and the main sequence and thermodynamics of sinusoidal and spiral phases. Kenzelmann and Harris objected that, under the exact crystal space group, different spin components belong to different irreducible representations and therefore should be treated as separate order parameters. This is formally correct at the crystallographic level, but it does not invalidate the model: when exchange interactions dominate over spin–orbit and lattice anisotropies, those components are approximately unified by spin-rotation symmetry into one vector order parameter, with the small symmetry-breaking terms incorporated phenomenologically. Thus the single-vector theory is an effective, economical description of the robust long-wavelength physics, even though material-specific refinements may require multiple irreducible order parameters.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an academic abstract for a paper responding to a comment on the continuum description of spiral multiferroics, mentioning general magnetic order, magnetically induced ferroelectricity, and magnetoelectric behavior.
counterfactuals.output: We respond to a recent Comment concerning the continuum description of spiral multiferroics. We clarify the assumptions, symmetry constraints, and range of validity of the phenomenological framework, emphasizing that it applies to general magnetic order rather than only to idealized single-\(\mathbf{q}\) spiral states. Within this approach, magnetically induced ferroelectricity arises from symmetry-allowed couplings between the electric polarization and spatially varying magnetic order, while uniform and modulated magnetic configurations are treated on equal footing. We further distinguish the emergence of a spontaneous polarization from the broader magnetoelectric behavior, which includes field-induced responses and polarization changes associated with magnetic reorientation or phase transitions. These considerations reconcile the continuum formulation with microscopic mechanisms and demonstrate its utility as a symmetry-based description of spiral and more general multiferroic phases.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
